The caption explicitly states that characteristic GPA pulmonary and destructive sinonasal lesions were absent, supporting attribution to relapsing polychondritis rather than GPA. panels.figure_caption: Enhanced CT of the neck and chest in a 46-year-old man presenting with a 2-month history of persistent fever, productive cough, and anterior chest pain. Physical examination revealed a recently developed saddle nose deformity; no auricular inflammation or peripheral arthritis was evident. Laboratory investigations demonstrated markedly elevated inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein 16.09 mg/dL; erythrocyte sedimentation rate 120 mm/h; ferritin peak 898 ng/mL). Serum anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) was repeatedly negative on screening assay, and both proteinase 3 (PR3)-ANCA and myeloperoxidase (MPO)-ANCA were negative on enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Renal function was normal (blood urea nitrogen 10.8 mg/dL; creatinine 0.61 mg/dL), and urinalysis showed no hematuria or proteinuria. Extensive microbiological workup, including blood cultures, tuberculosis assays, and viral panels, was unrevealing. Two months prior, the patient had been hospitalized at an outside hospital where broad-spectrum antibiotics had failed to control fever; he remained continuously febrile throughout the two-month interval, up to admission to our hospital. (A) Coronal CT image demonstrating diffuse smooth wall thickening and enhancement (red arrows) along the trachea and bilateral main bronchi. (B) Axial CT image at the level of the trachea showing circumferential wall thickening (red arrows). Chest CT showed no parenchymal nodules, cavities, or alveolar hemorrhage to suggest pulmonary granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) involvement. CT of the paranasal sinuses revealed only a retention cyst in the left sphenoid sinus, with no destructive sinonasal lesions to suggest GPA. Dynamic airway CT was not performed. The radiological report listed amyloidosis and GPA as differential diagnoses; relapsing polychondritis (RP) was not included. In light of the CT findings suspicious for GPA, further workup for IgG4-related disease and atypical infections was not pursued at that stage. GPA can cause indistinguishable tracheobronchial CT changes [1] and is ANCA-negative in approximately 10–20% of confirmed cases [2], rendering seronegative status uninformative. Meeting criteria for fever of unknown origin, whole-body 18F-FDG PET/CT was subsequently performed as part of the systematic evaluation [3].

(B and C) The trachea showed concentric narrowing, with the cartilage rings absent, indicating severe airway involvement. (D) The carina of the trachea demonstrated both mucosal hypertrophy and atrophy, suggesting advanced inflammatory damage. (E) The right main bronchus revealed mucosal thickening and slight narrowing of the lumen. (F) The right middle bronchus showed marked mucosal thickening with luminal narrowing. (G) The left main bronchus presented with significant mucosal thickening and narrowing, similar to the right bronchus. (H) The trachea during the expiratory phase displayed generalized inflammation and mucosal edema, resulting in a narrowed airway passage.

A: Bronchoscopy panel A in RP case with airway involvement showing arytenoid swelling, mapped to airway wall thickening; article title Early Diagnosis of Relapsing Polychondritis With Airway Involvement.
